content: Dr. Rukhsana Haider, employed by the Training and Assistance for Health and Nutrition (TAHN) Foundation in Dhaka, Bangladesh, was a member of the guideline development group. She participated in discussions regarding recommendations for the use of multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) for point-of-use fortification of foods consumed by pregnant women. However, she recused herself from voting on these recommendations. At the time of the meeting, Dr. Haider also served as a member of the Technical Advisory Group for Helen Keller International’s Assessment and Research on Child Feeding (ARCH) Project. It was agreed that she could fully engage in deliberations and decision-making on this recommendation. Dr. Maria Elena del Socorro Jefferds, employed by the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), disclosed her role as a co-investigator in a CDC-funded study on the effectiveness of micronutrient powders in Kenya. She is the lead author and co-author of several publications on this topic, including a special Sight and Life supplement on micronutrient powders published in 2013. She also participated in a UNICEF/CDC workshop on scaling up MNP interventions for children aged 6–23 months. Additionally, she coordinated and authored a monitoring manual for home fortification interventions, including MNPs, for the Home Fortification Technical Advisory Group (HF-TAG). Dr. Jefferds was an investigator in the first global assessment of home fortification interventions and the lead author of the corresponding report and related journal article, both published in 2013. She is also a co-author of a Cochrane systematic review of MNP interventions in children aged 6–23 months and 2–12 years. While she was allowed to participate in deliberations on recommendations related to MNPs, she recused herself from voting on recommendations concerning the use of MNPs for point-of-use fortification of foods. Dr. Lynette Neufeld disclosed that her current employer had received funding in the past four years for research and programming related to MNPs, although she was not leading any of these initiatives. In her previous position with a different employer, she was involved in research studies related to MNPs. She also declared her membership on the Steering Committee of HF-TAG. Dr. Neufeld was permitted to participate in deliberations on recommendations related to MNPs but recused herself from voting on recommendations concerning the use of MNPs for point-of-use fortification of foods. All other members of the guideline development group completed and signed written declarations of interest before the meeting and made verbal declarations of their interests during the meeting. These interests were deemed not relevant to the guideline on the use of MNPs for point-of-use fortification of foods consumed by pregnant women. External experts also declared their interests but did not participate in the deliberations or decision-making process. The WHO Secretariat will continue to monitor research developments in the area of micronutrient supplementation for pregnant women. If the guideline requires an update or if concerns arise regarding its validity, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will coordinate the update following the formal procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, along with its internal partners, will conduct a search for new evidence. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to evaluate in the guideline when it is due for review.
